original_title: Dragon Age's former producer had envisioned a 'Champions Edition' equivalent to Mass Effect's Legendary Edition, but he doesn't think it will happen anymore: 'There are basically no companies that could help you'
summary_en: A beloved fantasy RPG trilogy could have received the Mass Effect Legendary Edition treatment, but a former producer says the technical hurdles are too great. Fans hoping for a modern overhaul of Dragon Age's classic entries face a harsh reality.

en.title: Dragon Age Remaster? Former Producer Reveals Why It's Unlikely
en.summary: A beloved fantasy RPG trilogy could have received the Mass Effect Legendary Edition treatment, but a former producer says the technical hurdles are too great. Fans hoping for a modern overhaul of Dragon Age's classic entries face a harsh reality.
en.body:
The dream of a **Dragon Age: Champions Edition**, a unified remaster of **Dragon Age: Origins**, **Dragon Age 2**, and **Dragon Age: Inquisition**, has been a persistent hope for many fans. Much like **Mass Effect's Legendary Edition** revitalized Commander Shepard's saga for a new generation, many envisioned a similar loving touch for BioWare's epic fantasy series. However, former **Dragon Age** producer **Mark Darrah** has poured cold water on these aspirations, citing fundamental technological barriers that make such a project highly improbable.

Darrah, who has been vocal about the series' uncertain future following the reception of **Dragon Age: The Veilguard**, once envisioned a cohesive collection that would honor the heroes and lore spanning the trilogy. "I think what you want is a Champion's Edition," he previously stated, outlining a vision to combine the three distinct games into a single, polished experience. This would not only offer a convenient way for newcomers to dive into the world of Thedas but also allow long-time fans to relive their favorite moments with updated visuals and gameplay refinements. Unfortunately, the path to achieving this vision is far more complicated than it was for the **Mass Effect** trilogy.

## The Engine Conundrum

The primary obstacle lies in the engines used for each **Dragon Age** title. Unlike the **Mass Effect** games, which all benefited from the widely adopted and relatively consistent Unreal Engine, BioWare's **Dragon Age** games were built on a series of unique and evolving proprietary engines. **Dragon Age: Origins** utilized the Eclipse engine, an advancement of the Aurora Engine that also powered games like **The Witcher**. **Dragon Age 2** then moved to the further enhanced Lycium Engine, and **Dragon Age: Inquisition** famously ran on DICE's Frostbite engine. This lack of a unified technological foundation means that remastering each game would require vastly different approaches and toolsets. "There are basically no companies that could help you," Darrah explained, highlighting the scarcity of external expertise that could tackle such a fragmented technological landscape. The sheer effort and cost associated with rebuilding or heavily adapting these disparate engines for modern platforms would likely be prohibitive for publisher EA.

## A Fading Hope for Fans

For the dedicated **Dragon Age** community, this news is undoubtedly a disappointment. The desire for a polished, accessible way to experience the series' rich history is palpable. With **Dragon Age: The Veilguard** facing a challenging launch and BioWare undergoing significant changes, the prospect of revisiting the beloved older titles through a modern lens seemed like a viable way to keep the franchise in the spotlight. Yet, Darrah’s insights underscore the practical realities of game development and preservation. The technical debt accumulated across three different engine generations presents a formidable challenge, one that even a major publisher like EA may deem too risky or costly to undertake. This leaves fans to continue enjoying the games as they are, or to hope for a future where the technological barriers are somehow overcome.

## What's Next

Currently, there are no official announcements or plans regarding a **Dragon Age** remaster. BioWare's focus appears to be on future projects, though details remain scarce. Fans will have to wait and see if any further developments emerge.

content_raw: Things haven't looked great for Dragon Age since its latest entry, Dragon Age: The Veilguard was released to a mixed critical and muted commercial response back in 2024. EA subsequently laid off dozens of BioWare's staff, and numerous former developers have recently said they believe the series is probably dead. Yet, while there's little hope of a new Dragon Age game anytime soon (if ever), might there be a chance EA revisits the old Dragon Age games? The original Mass Effect trilogy got a spruced-up rerelease in its Legendary Edition back in 2021, despite the fact that EA hasn't exactly been desperate to push out new games in that series either (though a new one is apparently in the works, with the devs being too busy making it to talk about it ). Hence, could EA test players' appetite for Dragon Age with a similar remaster for Dragon Age: Origins , Dragon Age 2 , and Dragon Age: Inquisition ? Sadly, the chances of this happening are slim too, at least according to former Dragon Age producer Mark Darrah. In the same interview where he declared Dragon Age as probably dead, Darrah also pointed out that, while he had once envisioned a "Champion's Edition" equivalent to the Legendary Edition, EA is now unlikely to exhume the old games for a remaster due to the practical difficulties of doing so. Basically, it all comes down to technology. Where all three Mass Effect games ran on Unreal Engine, which is a widely used technology, the three Dragon Age games were all built on different engines. Dragon Age used BioWare's Eclipse engine—an upgraded version of the Aurora Engine (which was also used by CD Projekt for The Witcher ), Dragon Age 2 used the further enhanced Lycium Engine, while Dragon Age: Inquisition ran on DICE's Frostbite tech. "There's basically no one at BioWare any more that understands the Aurora Engine," Darrah told FRVR . "There's basically no one outside of BioWare anymore that understands the Aurora engine. So, unlike Mass Effect, which is Unreal, there are basically no companies that could help you." On top of this, Darrah reckons that such a remaster effort would require a new team, but claims that "EA doesn't like having employees, so, if you're going to do that, you're going to do that within the umbrella of BioWare, which means those people are not working on something else." That said, Darrah does think that a remaster of the original Dragon Age would sell well, mainly due to how it's a bit crusty around the edges today. "Dragon Age: Origins wasn't the most attractive game.
